title: 2 Samuel 16:1–4
context: Just past the summit of the Mount of Olives, Ziba, the steward of Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, meets David with donkeys and provisions. When David asks about Mephibosheth, Ziba claims his master stayed behind hoping to regain Saul's kingdom. David, in haste and distress, grants Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property. Later, Mephibosheth gives a very different account (2 Samuel 19:24–30).

verses.text: When David was a little past the top, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with a couple of donkeys saddled, and on them two hundred loaves of bread, and one hundred clusters of raisins, and one hundred summer fruits, and a container of wine.
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba meets David with donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit, and wine. Arminian readers note the welcome generosity of the gift in a moment of need, while the following verses raise questions about Ziba's motives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing for David in the wilderness through unexpected means. They also note that providential provision can come through people whose motives are mixed or self-serving.

verses.text: The king said to Ziba, “What do you mean by these?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on; and the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat; and the wine, that those who are faint in the wilderness may drink.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba explains the gifts are for the king's household and those faint in the wilderness. Arminian readers note that the provisions meet real needs, and David's people would have welcomed them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the practical kindness of the provisions. God's care for his anointed reaches to food and rest, the ordinary necessities of a people on the move.

verses.text: The king said, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is staying in Jerusalem; for he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will restore me the kingdom of my father.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba claims Mephibosheth said, "Today the house of Israel will restore me the kingdom of my father." Arminian readers note that this accusation is later disputed by Mephibosheth (19:26), leaving readers to weigh both accounts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the conflicting testimony. Mephibosheth later says, "my servant deceived me" (19:26). Scripture records both claims, and readers should be cautious about accepting Ziba's version.

verses.text: Then the king said to Ziba, “Behold, all that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours.” Ziba said, “I bow down. Let me find favor in your sight, my lord, O king.”
verses.arminianNotes: David grants Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property. Arminian readers see a hasty judgment made in distress, a warning about deciding on one side of a story without hearing the other.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David later revises this ruling, dividing the land (19:29). Even God's anointed king can judge wrongly under pressure, a reminder that human rulers are fallible.
